parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek αξόνι (axóni). Doublet of akson.
From Greek μάχη (máchi), from Ancient Greek μάχη (mákhē). Occurs exclusively in the Arbëresh dialect.

parole.significato: large tray or container made of bronze
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek απλάδα (apláda, “(metal) tray, platter”).

Borrowed from Greek αρχάγγελος (archángelos), less likely via Bulgarian архангел (arhangel). The 8th of November (in the Julian Calendar, corresponding to 21st of November in the Gregorian calendar), is traditionally celebrated the synaxis of the Archangel Michael and Other Bodiless Powers. Doublet
Recent borrowing from Greek μπακαλιάρος (bakaliáros, “cod”), from Dutch bakkeljauw.

parole.significato: A friendly exclamation to a person.
parole.testo: From Greek βρε (vre), from Greek μωρέ (moré, “stupid”, vocative). Doublet of more.
From Greek τσεκούρι (tsekoúri, “axe”), ultimately from Latin securis (“axe”). See there for more details.
From Greek τσιμπίδα (tsimpída), from Albanian cimb.
From an intermediate variant ciron + diminutive -kë, from Greek τσιρόνι (tsiróni), itself of blurry origin.
Borrowed from Greek δεμάτι (demáti, “sheaf”). Doublet of demet.
Borrowed from Greek διδαχή (didachí). First attested in 1764 in the Codex of Berat and nowhere else: "...kishin ardhurë të dëgjoinë dhidhaqinë [e] ti...". The term is used exclusively in Orthodoxy.
Borrowed from Greek δρόγγος (dróngos), from Ancient Greek γόγγρος (góngros). Doublet of gru.
Singularized plural of *domatë, from Greek ντομάτα (ntomáta).
Coined by Naum Veqilharxhi. From do (“to love”) + nder (“honour”) + -ës. Calque of Greek φιλότιμος (filótimos).

Borrowed from Greek γύφτος (gýftos, “Gipsy”), with regressive metathesis of the f, from Ancient Greek Αἰγύπτιος (Aigúptios, “Egyptian”). For the apparent, and possibly coincidental, retention of the initial /e/, compare Aromanian gheghiftu.
Borrowed from Greek φιλονικώ (filonikó), aorist φιλονίκησα (filoníkisa).
Originally a Tosk-only word. Borrowed from Greek φιόγκος (fiógkos). Doublet of flok and fjok.
Possibly borrowed from Greek φόρα (fóra, “pace; impetus”), compare the expression παίρνω φόρα (paírno fóra, “gain courage”).
Compare Greek φούστα (foústa) and Romanian fustă.
From (the stem of) Greek καβούρι (kavoúri, “crab”) and suffix -e.

parole.significato: gargling, gargle (act of cleaning one's mouth by holding water or some other liquid in the back of the mouth and blowin…
parole.testo: Ultimately derived from Greek γαργάρα (gargára, “gargling, gargle”).
From Greek γείτονας (geítonas, “neighbour”). The collective gjitoni is derived thereafter.
From Greek γειτονία (geitonía). Possibly from gji + tonë
Borrowed from Greek χώρα (chóra, “town, country”). See also Greek χωριό (chorió, “village”) and Aromanian hoarã (“village”).
Borrowed from Greek ηγεμόνας (igemónas). Doublet of hegjemon.

parole.significato: A prefixoid denoting sharpness, roughness, abruptness and/or curvity.
parole.testo: Uncertain. Likely akin to Greek κατσο- (katso-) and possibly borrowed from it. Alternatively from kec, kac (“goat, lamb”).
Uncertain. Possibly from kaca- + Greek γκέλα (gkéla).
A relatively old borrowing from Greek κατσί (katsí).
From Greek καπίστρι (kapístri), from Latin capistrum.
Borrowed from Greek κρίνο n (kríno), dialectal κρίνα f (krína, “lily”).
Borrowed from Greek χρυσό γαϊτάνι (chrysó gaïtáni, “golden braid”).
Tosk, Arvanitika; with variant kunave, from Greek κουναδι (kounadi), κουνάβι (kounávi).
Borrowed from Greek κουρούπι (kouroúpi), κουρουπί (kouroupí, “clay pot”), dialectally “clay beehive”.
Related to Turkish kutu, Serbo-Croatian kùtija, Bulgarian кути́я (kutíja), Romanian cutie, all with the same meaning. Ultimately derived from Greek κουτί (koutí).

parole.significato: to fuck, to have intercourse with

parole.testo: From këputë (“sole”). Other proposals include: 1) Camarda, from Greek παπούτσι (papoútsi). 2) Meyer, from Turkish papuç pabuç, from Ottoman Turkish پاپوش (papush), from Classical Persian پاپوش (pāpōš), although these are less probable as they are reflected already in Albanian papuçë.
Borrowed from Greek έλαθησα (élathisa), from λαθαίνω (lathaíno, “I err”).
From Greek λαπαρός (laparós) (compare Bulgarian лапардосвам (lapardosvam)). Less likely from lapër + -os.
Borrowed from Greek λευτερώνω (lefteróno), variant of ελευθερώνω (eleftheróno).
From Greek *λογαρίζω (*logarízo), a variant of λογαριάζω (logariázo).
From Greek λογή (logí, “sort”). Related to llogaris.

A borrowing from Greek λοστός (lostós, “lever, bar”), which is also seen in Bulgarian-Macedonian лосm "bar". The final syllable was perceived as a postfixed article during the borrowing process or was omitted through the morphological borrowing process. Orel incorrectly derived it from the verb loz

parole.significato: introduces a down-scaled desire. at least
parole.testo: From Greek μακάρι (makári, “if only, I wish”). Compare Romanian măcar (“at least, not even”).
Borrowed from Greek μανουσάκι (manousáki), see there for more. Doublet of menekshe.
From Greek εμποδίζω (empodízo) via incorporation as an -is verb.
First attested as mrīmagë; borrowed from Greek μυρμήγκι (myrmígki, “ant”). According to Kristofordhi and Mihăescu, a borrowing from Doric Greek μύρμαξ (múrmax)
Borrowed from Greek μουρνταρεύω (mourntarévo), aorist μουρντάρεψα (mourntárepsa).

Borrowed from Greek αναφορά (anaforá), ναφορά (naforá). Compare Romanian anaforă, naforă, Aromanian anafurã, nafurã, fanfurã, Serbo-Croatian nàfora /на̀фора, Macedonian нафора (nafora), Bulgarian на́фора (náfora).

parole.significato: to lull, sing a lullaby to, put to sleep
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek νανουρίζω (nanourízo), aorist νανούρισα (nanoúrisa).
From Greek νοικοκύρης (noikokýris, “head of household”), (compare νοικοκυρά (noikokyrá, “housewife”).
Borrowed from Greek παίδα (paída). First attested in the 18th century.
Borrowed from Greek παλαμάρι (palamári) and Ottoman Turkish پالامار (palamar).

parole.significato: a dull, passive man, whose excess of health has caused him to lose his usual agility. Used as an insult.
parole.testo: Possibly from Greek παλούκι (paloúki, “stake, pole, pale”).

parole.significato: to fall down on (something) suddenly, covering it completely
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek πλακώνω (plakóno). Compare Aromanian plucosescu.
Borrowed from Greek πουρνάρι /πρινάρι (pournári), from Ancient Greek πρῖνος (prînos).
From Greek κυβερνώ (kyvernó) with vowel assimilation.
From Greek κύμινον (kýminon, “cumin”), ultimately from Semitic.

parole.significato: king in a pack of playing cards
parole.testo: From Greek ρήγας (rígas), cognate with the also borrowed Romanian rigă. Ultimately from Latin rex, thus forming a doublet of regj.

parole.significato: wooden donkey saddle (packsaddle), as opposed to shalë
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek σαμάρι (samári, “wooden donkey saddle, packsaddle”).

parole.significato: to cover (the dead) with a shroud, to enshroud
parole.testo: Borrowed from Greek σαβανώνω (savanóno), aorist σαβάνωσα (savánosa). By surface analysis, savan + -os.

Orel suggests Greek σπάργανα (spárgana), σπάργανο (spárgano). However, due to the sp - shp evolution and the n - r rhotacism pattern between Gheg and Tosk that only exists in old borrowing, suggest older borrowing such as Ancient Greek σπάργανον (spárganon)
From Greek σκύλος (skýlos, “dog”) + -e (feminine suffix) (cf. feminine dhelpër (“id.”)).
In the -ng- forms, borrowed from Greek σπάγγος (spángos). In the -g- forms, borrowed from Italian spago directly.
From Greek σπινάκιον (spinákion) or Italian spinacio, ultimately from Classical Persian اسپناخ (ispanāx).
Borrowed from Greek στέρνα (stérna). Doublet of cisternë.
Borrowed from Greek στρώμα (stróma). Compare strugë, strum, shtrungë.

First attested in the old definite ablative in the Mëshari of Buzuku as fermeshit Borrowed from Greek θρύμμα (thrýmma, “crumb; fragment”), akin to Romanian fărâmă, Aromanian sãrmã. The verb thërrmoj (“to crumble, shatter”) was presumably coined in Albanian and borrowed into Balkan Romance as Aromani
From Greek τριαντάφυλλο (triantáfyllo). Compare Romanian trandafir, Aromanian trandafilã, Ukrainian троянда (trojanda).
Variant of barkë. Borrowed from Greek βάρκα (várka), from Late Latin barca.
Borrowed from Greek βούλα (voúla), from Latin bulla.

Either from zemër with the meaning of 'centre of the day', or from the same root of Greek ημέρα (iméra, “day”), although the initial anlaut z- remains unexplained. A borrowing from Greek διήμερον (diímeron, “period of twenty-four hours”) is not excluded.
